utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, can the case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-97-24-PT, Prosecutor versus Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, for the Prosecution I am Michael Keegan. I am assisted by my colleagues Ms. Ann Sutherland, Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff and Mr. Morten Bergsmo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honour. For the Defence, Dusan Vucicevic, and I am assisted by my co-counsel, Mr. Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The defendant is in court. Can I make sure that he can hear the proceedings and it is being translated in a language which he understands. Dr. Kovacevic, can you understand? You do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, it is your motion today that we are going to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, indeed it is a Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the material which you have sent and you can take it that we read that. Your last letter indicates that you will not be calling medical evidence. I do not think that there are any matters on which we would wish to hear any medical witnesses, and I do not believe the Prosecution want to call any medical evidence. Is that the position as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to comport with previous orders of the Trial Chamber, it is the understanding of the Defence that the parties have been granted only the right to cross-examine the evidence against them, and to that effect, we understand the court's decision, and we do not intend to call the prosecuting witnesses for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That being so, we will hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court, the Office of the Prosecutor, Defence motion for the provisional release turns on this Chamber's pronouncement of law and reconciling of law that the previous decisions of this Tribunal have addressed. In Blaskic, Delalic, Delic and Landzo cases. Even though those interpretations as submitted by the Prosecutor are very similar, but yet they leave enough room for this Trial Chamber to reconcile them with the basic doctrine of the Article 21.3 of the Statute, which is named "presumption of innocence". There is ever-present opposition between those two instruments that govern decisions of this Tribunal, Article 21 and Rule 65. With presumption of innocence, the burden for prolonged confinement with ever-increasing duration of time shifts on Prosecution to justify such extensive confinement. While Rule 65, if interpreted literally, gives unlimited right, unabridged right, unfettered discretion, for the Prosecutor and the court to keep the defendant in detention. However, our submission, supported by the facts will indicate that not only the exceptional circumstances will turn on the totality of the medical facts of the defendant Dr. Kovacevic, but also on the reasonable suspicion or lack thereof from the day that Dr. Kovacevic was arrested until the very day that we are in court today. In the Delalic case, the Trial Chamber opined: "The gravity of the offence with which the person is charged before the International Tribunal is self-evident." To hold such a dicta as self-evident throughout the sessions of this Tribunal, no matter how long it might be, would be an error. It was such a blanket endorsement of any decision by the Office of the Prosecutor, or by any errors of the confirming judge, would deny presumption of innocence, would deny due process and would deny justice to somebody who is innocently accused, or, to let me be more circumspect, your Honour, to somebody whose indictment does not have a scintilla of evidence pointing to his personal intent to aid and abet and further the crime the alleged crime of which he has been charged. If we do not change this premise, we will face a chance to render impossible decisions, and unjust decisions. Therefore, all our submissions are intended to help this Trial Chamber to reach a fair and just decision. The Delalic case also makes conclusion of law that burden of proof rests upon the Defence to rebut the presumption of innocence, or in other words, the burden of proof in this motion, even on the very element of the merits of the case, that means a reasonable suspicion, defendant has right to bring new evidence to rebut that reasonable suspicion was indeed reasonable, even though as a matter of law we disagree with this -- respectfully disagree with this conclusion of law, but arguendo, with the facts that we are about to present, even this conclusion of law would suffice to find, to support the finding of this Trial Chamber that there was no reasonable suspicion to indict, and even more, to further hold Dr. Kovacevic in the detention unit of this Tribunal. The Prosecutor in his brief is asserting that the law which this Trial Chamber ought to consider in deciding upon this motion should be disjointed. On one hand under 65(A) the Trial Chamber should decide solely upon the medical evidence. On another hand, like in the Landzo case, they should consider the length of detention and reasonableness of the crime committed and all other elements separately. By their own submission of law this is incorrect, because the case that they have cited, Hardy versus United Kingdom, indicates that all facts must be considered and the plain reading, which is the guiding light of courts throughout the world, it is plain reading of the Statute, indicates that 65(A) says the court has power to decide, and second, the court has power to find what exceptional circumstances are. In such a very complex discretional area, I respectfully suggest that our proposition of law be adopted and all the factors be considered, because that would be the only fair and just means to decide upon the issues before your Honours. Your Honours, I would turn and analyse certain submissions that we have made, the Defence have made in our brief, against certain submissions that the Prosecutor has submitted, because of the time constraints that both parties have been exposed to, the facts contained in reports that have been filed to the court on 14th January, only two days ago, could not have reasonably entered into it. Therefore I will try to compare and contrast, so that one can supplement my argument with the facts that have been filed before the court according to court order schedule. The first element in the consideration of this motion is whether there is a reasonable suspicion, and what reasonable suspicion is has been delineated in the Delic case. That reasonable suspicion has to be a finding of the court. In reviewing the file of Dr. Kovacevic before this Tribunal, there is no one shred of evidence that points that he had an intent to commit this crime, and this indeed, a high crime that he had allegedly committed and that had allegedly occurred requires an intent, and even more so intent at the time of armed conflict. We have noted that at the hearing before, in our brief we have submitted and put the Prosecutor on notice that element of intent is missing and what did the court get in return? The court in return had gotten the submission, an exhibit to their brief, which is basically 35, 30 pages or so finding of fact from Tadic case, the only defendant that has been so far convicted before this Tribunal. However, that defendant's charge was not the same charge facing Dr. Kovacevic. Dr. Kovacevic was not represented in that case. The finding of fact, most importantly, of the Trial Chamber in that case does not even once mention the name "Dr. Kovacevic". How could that be relevant? This time, your Honours, I move that that exhibit be stricken as irrelevant. Looking back at the law pronouncements of this Tribunal, reasonableness of suspicion and degree of culpability of the defendant must be weighed at times of the hearing on the motion for provisional release, and be considered in such a fashion the high of the culpability, the higher the burden of proof or exceptional circumstances. With due respect, your Honours, without any evidence that Prosecutor has adduced either before the confirming judge or at any time later, our burden should be minimum. However, with the totality of the medical facts, somatic, cardiac, hypertension, brain damage, functional brain changes; Dr. Kovacevic and his Defence are ready to meet even the highest burden. I cannot leave the area of the reasonable suspicion so lightly, because it is basically an element of intent of this crime which the Defence see first if the Prosecution will have to show that indeed that Dr. Kovacevic voluntarily joined an enterprise whose plan was to commit the alleged crimes. Second, it should be is that he intended to aid and abet and further these crimes, and the third, finally, that the alleged crimes had been committed. So far the Prosecution has failed at every stage before the court to meet the burden on any of these. While the Prosecution was confirming hastily this indictment on March 13th 1997, they would come before Judge Odio Benito saying that United Nations forces or any other forces on the ground will have a chance to pick up these accused, so please confirm it, and they hardly gave her any evidence and the evidence that was given was basically the evidence of indictments of the other persons, and some conclusory statements by Mr. Reid, which I have cited in my brief. My view that free speech, that was only elements there exercising, indicating that Dr. Kovacevic was exercising his right to free speech. Those statements when translated properly do not even indicate that that free speech amounted to incitement to commit the alleged crime of genocide. There was another statement that Dr. Kovacevic, I have put it in my brief, that he was at a press conference. However, Dr. Kovacevic -- we want to be candid to this court, because Dr. Kovacevic wants to be exonerated of these charges and the only way is to be as candid as possible, because the truth must prevail. Dr. Kovacevic, as we submitted, was appointed by multi-ethnic municipal assembly to the position of the president of the municipal executive board, unanimously. He has realised the informal conversations, an attorney, a classmate of his a few days later, that his authority will be to make 10 or 15 per cent of decisions and all other decisions are handed down to them by the state. So his actual responsibilities were health, elementary education and communal services. The doctor was busy in the hospital, and that is the irrefutable evidence that we are presenting to you today, your Honours. That evidence of a doctor, a healer, who puts his hands on all the patients, all the people to come to him, regardless of the ethnic background, of the nationality, and there are several hundreds of those names that are submitted to you today. That report has been certified by the director, by the present director of the hospital, therefore we submit it as a veritable and credible evidence. Moreover, we are submitting to you the copies of the operating-room logs from the Prijedor hospital. What do they show us? They show us the daily work when Dr. Kovacevic showed up and performed the services that he knows best, providing anaesthesia for patients undergoing surgeries. If you would be kind enough to look at the schedules that we submitted, and somehow we submitted it and the Registrar copied up, if you look from the last page up, chronologically, it seems they have been transposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are the exhibits to your memorandum?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. You may look, page 1175, S file, indicates the name of Radzin Marema and Kadziric Basia, I believe, but the first name I cannot pronounce, or cannot read correctly. On April 24 1992 -- these are Muslim people. We natives of Yugoslavia could tell the people by their names. They were given anaesthesia by Dr. Kovacevic. If you flip the page, then on 26th April 1992, Begovic Alijana, last name I cannot read here, but first name is Ahmet, it is a Muslim name, were given anaesthesia again by Dr. Kovacevic. If you look on the next page, your Honours, this is now in May, I believe that was 1st May, Dr. Kovacevic again had given anaesthesia to Emina Kadic, and we can go on and on. On the next page, Dr. Kovacevic had anaesthetised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The page is 1181.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: 1181, Dr. Kovacevic. Your Honours, we have for your perusal circled, because those pages are -- there are two pages that go to one page of the protocol, and for purposes of our copying, we have copied them in this fashion, but on the right-hand page there would be name of the anaesthetist, on the left-hand page that would be the name of the patient. Names of the patients and dates and the names of the anaesthetist have been encircled. Each and every page indicates that there was Dr. Kovacevic present at work and they were one or more Muslim patients operated on and there was no discrimination or bigotry of any kind displayed by Dr. Kovacevic at that time. Your Honours, this irrebutable evidence goes a long way to show his intent, whether or not to harm or to heal, his fellow citizens of Prijedor. The Prosecutor has failed even to bring any names, any witnesses who have stated that Dr. Kovacevic has harmed them, or had spoken in any way to harm them. There is only one statement as I can remember, your Honour, supposedly Mr. Nazirovic, a witness in the Tadic case, was testifying that he overheard Dr. Kovacevic calling from outside a small radio station and cursing, and I read those both statements, your Honour, in Serbo-Croatian and in English, and it is a travesty, your Honour. There are a lot of swear words in Serbian and even if he did call, he could not have said those, because originally they do not make sense, they are never used, and they are products of fabrications. When fabrication is original English is being translated, it just sounds like a fabrication, something the world media, pandering to the frenzy of world media. Your Honour, we sincerely intend, with your high office and with our candour, we will bring this case finally before justice. There was nothing else that links this fine doctor and this humanist, to the alleged crime charged. But I will move on and on, your Honour, because after being arrested, the doctor's medical condition has deteriorated so severely and has deteriorated gradually. We have received reports from Dutch doctors that were treating Dr. Kovacevic while he was in jail and one of the first reports was dated July 18th, 1997, signed by Dr. Haeck, internist, who makes a finding: "Dr. Kovacevic's blood pressure has changed between 170 and 200 and 130 diastolic." By all standards way too high. Even though he has examined the doctor, on that day he found, if you look at page -- there was an exhibit to the Prosecutor's brief, and page 2, he is reading blood pressures in supine, meaning the doctor is standing on the right side and the left side of the arm. The blood pressures are 190 on 110, 190 on 110 constantly, 190 on 150 on the left side. In lying position they are even higher. That is after being seven days in the detention unit, after suffering two strokes, one on 10th July and one on the -- we do not exactly know whether on 15th or 17th but certainly before this good doctor examined him and this good doctor made the finding that indeed that stroke has happened. Having been exposed to a doctor who should be practising good medicine, but yet the results are non-sufficient, inadequate, and the doctor who is treating him, he is aware of that. When you look at his conclusion, he said: "At this moment, hypertensive and anticoagulant treatment is being optimised." He is doing the best he could: "However, his blood pressure is probably also influenced by the stress of being imprisoned in a foreign country and being separated from his family." That statement goes early on, that is a statement dated July 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you can help us, what is "CVA" and a "TIA"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. CVA is "cerebro-vascular accident", a plain old word "stroke". TIA is "transient iscimic attack". Your Honour, Dr. Haeck has found that Dr. Kovacevic's heart is not beating regularly. This irregular beating of the heart is producing the clotting on the left side of the heart, and it is showering the brain directly with these small thrombi. TIA are clinical effects of these multiple thrombi being showered to his brain. That is why good Dr. Haeck is prescribing anticoagulant medications that he has put in his conclusion, and he has also listed on the medicines that he has treated. But I have really to commend Dr. Haeck. He has put on his findings of medication dosages of the drugs Verapamil, Digitalis, Renitec, Tenormin, Escar, and there is no dosage of Marcoumar. That is a drug that is a blood-thinner, that is a drug that could kill, that is a drug that even now in jail he receives a test every week to control how thin is his blood. If too thick, he is going to have a stroke; if too thin, he will die from bleeding in the brain. It is indeed serious. But the doctor was not given that information. Somebody just did not think it was important. The next report that Prosecution is submitting is the report of Dr. Augusta Reviere, cardiologist, which basically confirms the previous findings. Again it seems, you know, dosages of the anticoagulant drug is not known, high blood pressure is there, it is noted. There is enlargement of his heart, they are confirming that they are emboli, thrombi that are going to his brain. This doctor is noting this, third sentence from the bottom on the page 2 of Dr. Reviere's report: "With the above mentioned situation in mind, the therapy at the moment is well chosen for the anti-hypertension, but both Verapamil and Tenormin have a negative ionotropic effect on the left ventricular wall." That, your Honours, means we are treating his blood pressure, but we are making his heart weaker. Our good doctor Kovacevic is suffering, he cannot breathe, he is short of breath, he cannot move. He is feeling that something is not being done right. It has taken from this report, delivered on July 18th through 25th November for this therapy that was suspected wrong at that time to be changed, upon assistance of Defence and several motions to finally obtain cardiac catheterisation to diagnose doctor had heart attack and his heart was weak and it could not pump. I am not suggesting the doctor did it intentionally, I am not suggesting the doctors do not know, but in the best hands, omissions do happen, but why do omissions happen for the person that is in jail? But what I would like to focus your attention on, your Honours, is that we do not have a layman. If there was a layman that never would have been noticed. Maybe nothing would have been changed, maybe he would be dead by now, we would not have to be here. But he had noticed that something is not happening that was supposed to happen. He was getting weaker, he was getting more shortness of breath and he has asked his Defence team to help, and we do thank this Trial Chamber in hearing our pleas so that all those tests have been performed. Based on these tests, Dr. Dijkman on November 25th had changed some therapy, he had added Digoxin, which is a drug that enhances contractability, the strength of the muscle. He replaced Isoptin, which the doctor had from the very beginning, which may have been making his heart weaker. But what happened? His blood pressure did not change and the main culprit, the problem that is driving all his conditions is his blood pressure that is not being treated. Blood pressure has ruined his heart, aortosclerosis has clogged up the arteries of his heart. Dr. Dijkman, to his own surprise, has found that right coronary artery is completely occluded. What it means is that the right side of the heart does not function, it is a scar, so the heart beats with two sides and the third side is going the other way. What Professor Ostojic from Belgrade clearly described in his report that Dr. Kovacevic's heart contracted, it is bigger than the heart of a normal person at rest. That is why he is weak, that is why he cannot exercise. That is why he is preoccupied with thoughts of death, because his life expectancy is at best four to five, but he may die within this year, with incidence of 30 to 40 per cent. Those are the facts, your Honour, submitted by Professor Ostojic of Belgrade. Professor Ostojic, as we submit in his CV, is a well published and well respected professor of cardiology who has lectured in all European cities, he has been a visiting professor of cardiology in the United States. But let us look now how these ongoing continuous, unsolvable problems that are making an invalid of him, have affected his mind, believing while working in Western Europe, not far from here, in suburbs of Disolo for five years when he became a specialist anaesthesiologist, he has learned that modern effective medicine and caring doctors could solve the problems of hypertension, but yet his hypertension has not been treated. He has been made a mockery of, and I refer you to the facts in the report of Dr. -- psychiatrist from Texas, Lorraine Sommerfeldt, where she is stating that while Dr. Kovacevic, while asking an internist at the detention unit why he has bleeding on his leg, the doctor said, "you bumped it", but doctor, knowing that he is of a blood thinner, the very first bleeding could mean that you are going overboard, the next bleeding could be the brain, but response from the doctor in jail was "do not worry, you will not bump your head, that will not happen". That is cynicism, and for a man who is in jail, who feels that he is being medically neglected, mind you, your Honours, that is his feeling but the outcome of the treatment is very close to it, that he is being made a mockery of, has lost faith, has retreated in himself, has been self-medicating, has developed depression, fears and ideations, which Dr. Sommerfeldt called paranoid, because he cannot assist his doctors in the treatment furthermore, his thinking is profoundly depressive and we had a good doctor from London, Dr. Bowden, who has spent three hours with Dr. Kovacevic and two hours inspecting the prison and talking to the deputy warden, who basically only made less than one page and a few sentences in psychiatric findings, saying "there is nothing wrong with Dr. Kovacevic". But what struck me, the very first page, the very first sentence of that finding, was predicated upon the incorrect translation, and good Dr. Bowden is going to go on a steady road and look on the consequences of Dr. Kovacevic's psychiatric suffering indicated by stress in the past from which he almost died, went the other way. Let me just find this, your Honours, so we can set the record straight on this point. On page 7 of Dr. Bowden's report, it says "past medical history": "Dr. Kovacevic said that in about 1979 he had an episode of nephritis." I will editorialise a little bit. Nephritis is an infection of the kidneys: "... which required hospitalisation in Germany. Routine investigation at that time showed that he had healed gastritis." Dr. Kovacevic never had a kidney problem. Dr. Kovacevic was working in the first six months in Germany, that was evidenced in Dr. Lorraine Sommerfeldt's report, and being alone without his family he developed haemorrhagic bleeding gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach, which is a quintessential symptom of somatisation of a stress disorder, and he spent a month in the hospital trying to heal that and the problem got contained when his son and his wife came and stayed with him. If Dr. Bowden became aware of such a fact, perhaps he would have talked when he investigated the mood, he would not have been so short and curt. His effect was normal. Dr. Sommerfeldt is finding different. But your Honours, let me step back for one second. It is not my intention to criticise doctors. It is my intention to help you apply the law to these very complex facts, and in the Landzo case, the Trial Chamber found that they do have a power to pick and choose between the reports, stack the votes, two to one, two to one you lose. That is a rather simplistic approach, your Honours, because the law turns on the facts and expert witnesses testifying in direct testimony by the order of this court on these facts, I think it would be very proper for the courts to compare and contrast these facts. If Dr. Bowden had had a report of Dr. Elsman appointed by the Registry, he would not have made this finding, because Dr. Elsman agreed with Dr. Sommerfeldt. Dr. Elsman and Dr. Sommerfeldt both say that Dr. Kovacevic has an acute psychiatric condition which needs to be treated. However, Dr. Bowden's presentation indicates that he has received a copy of the indictment which the other two doctors did not, and not only that, but he had received the voluminous finding of fact from Tadic's case, from Mr. Keegan, Prosecutor, which does not have one word of Dr. Kovacevic. Well, any sensitive human being, doctor, could easily be prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I thought you were not going to attack the doctors. You now seem to be doing that. I do not know that we are going to be helped by that. I think too that in fact, so the record should be straight, that although it is right that Dr. Elsman came to a conclusion about the medical condition, he found no psychotic disorder. He did find a stress disorder. I am looking at the last page of his report, page 4. He thought that some form of psychotherapy is indicated, but he came to the conclusion that the psychiatric condition of the accused is compatible with his continued detention. But I suppose your answer to that is we should not say two to one and therefore we accept the two as against the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am asking you to look into the conditions upon which these examinations have been -- Dr. Bowden has taken three hours to examine the client, Dr. Sommerfeldt has taken five and a half hours to examine the client, Dr. Elsman has taken one hour. So what Dr. Elsman is using very cautious language, he is not denying there might be the possibility of suicidal tendencies. Let me just get to that page, your Honour. Okay, I am here, "the subject feels very low".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I am reading from page 3. Then it is 2/1472, that is as filed with the Office of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: He says: "The subject feels very low, but there are no symptoms of depression in the narrower sense. There are no indications" -- he did not say there are no suicidal tendencies, he said there are no indications of suicidal tendencies. But then the next paragraph says: "The subject is very tense and tends to exercise self-control in putting on a brave face." So the doctor is using cautionary language; if this patient is not open to me, I am not quite sure whether he might or not attempt to kill himself. The doctor, was pressed for time, of course, so you know at the beginning, trying to get a little more about background, he is stating Dr. Kovacevic is a member of a Catholic Orthodox -- he celebrated Catholic Orthodox Christmas, so I do not know what is context of such a statement, but sending that to Dr. Kovacevic, who is a very religious man, could have led to Dr. Kovacevic, just as Dr. Elsman concluded, to close up and not show his emotions to him. On the contrary, statement by Dr. Sommerfeldt indicates that Dr. Kovacevic was expressing his emotion, he was tearful. Dr. Sommerfeldt had supported each and every finding or each and every conclusion by the question asked in the matters when she evaluated mood, when she evaluated judgement, when she evaluated intellectual ability, all those she found to be decreased, and most importantly, when she was evaluated whether or not he has any paranoid or suicidal tendencies, she asked this doctor -- very specific and very provoking question. Just here, the evaluation of Dr. Elsman and Dr. Bowden show that Dr. Kovacevic is a man of higher intelligence, while not fully opening to Dr. Elsman and not opening at all to Dr. Bowden, he has poured his heart to Dr. Sommerfeldt, and he indicated, not directly, because being so proud, that he is thinking about death all the time, expressing his views through philosophy that he is reading now. Your Honours, in evaluating the facts of these findings of the psychiatry experts, there is a common thread. There is a thread of stress, inappropriate reaction to stress in the past. There is a medical severe disabling and life-limiting medical condition which was inadequately treated while in confinement, without, and I am suggesting this without one scintilla of the blame, this is to advance the cause of Dr. Kovacevic's health, which Dr. Kovacevic, being a very intelligent man, has realised, trying to correct to no avail, and became depressed, became unable to communicate and take and follow the orders of his doctors, as Dr. Sommerfeldt said, "he has not been taking the pills as he was directed". We are at the point that he has expressed ideas of doing away with himself, because he feels there was no justice, he feels there is no medical treatment, he feels that his life is only four years to live and even if he receives the justice, he might receive ultimately a sentence that this court cannot impose and that is a death sentence, because there is a death stalking for him while he is in the detention unit, and even if he lives throughout those four years, he might go through trial, we sincerely believe, be acquitted and die. This is very harsh sentence for the regulatory purpose of the detention. Your Honours, we leave his life at your mercy, but we have to go on and proceed to the next element, the next requirement upon Rule 65. That requirement is if released, would Dr. Kovacevic harm any witnesses? In the other cases decided by the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal, we are talking about young men with criminal history, with convictions, with clear evidence in the indictment they have committed violence or led military charges or harmed civilians. None of those elements are present in the history of Dr. Kovacevic. As a matter of fact, there is evidence, while the others were maiming and killing, that he was helping. Than an unsupported conclusion that an accused could harm a witness is not enough to stand before the due process of law which he is entitled to in order to be released. It has to be some connection. As a matter of fact, we really have not received any witness at all, name of any witness that had accused him, let alone that any witness that lives in Prijedor area, so there would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence be asked to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Even if we could let our image raise a doctor, never be in charge of anything in his life, could harm anybody, but more importantly your Honours, the very nature of the crime that he is charged with requires complicit association, and if the doctor is here and other alleged co-conspirators are at large, those witnesses, if there is any fear, would have to be concerned from others but not the doctor. Would this Dr. Kovacevic return back to his trial to have his day in court? He has nothing else in his life to live for than to clear his good name and his family name. He has lived his life, as we see in the reports. An unfair blemish has been placed in him by off-handedly confirming the indictment. He has not been given a chance like other indictees to surrender, which he would have. All what would he need if this court shows the mercy and let him be treated at home just to have an Office of the Registry or whoever place a call and Dr. Kovacevic would come in. But we have assurances of government of Dr. Biljana Plavsic, now indeed very co-operative with the international forces securing peace in Bosnia, that they are going to assist this honourable court in implementation of any conditions of the temporary release that the court may impose. Some other cases that we mentioned already have been discussing that there might be neighbouring countries which do not co-operate with this Tribunal, but times -- if I may cite former President Roosevelt, there is nothing worse from fear than fear itself. We cannot fear in the abstract. He has been stigmatised. All what he had, worked for, in the words of the psychiatrist, it was his good name, to what he highly adheres and for him to run, to run for himself, he would only run to his own grave where he would place himself. He has no other way than to place -- than to go to any future but through your courtroom, your Honours. However, objectively there is NATO forces in Prijedor, there is international police force, there is a local police and the command of Ms. Plavsic and even policemen itself of Plavsic government, with the seat in Banja Luka, which is extremely co-operative now, which is in that home town. They are all willing to co-operate and impose orders, implement whatever conditions, restrictions you would impose. Dr. Kovacevic is willing and quite happy to stay under home arrest, to report to any authorities that you may desire, and come back. Not to leave home town, home county, not to associate with any persons that Prosecutor and the court so designs. He needs peace and quiet and family support to heal his mind and to control the medical ailments that are making his condition so grave. Indeed, your Honours, you do have an example in his past. He stayed alive after that bout with Dresden in Germany. Even as a young man, he is too old now. Your Honours, it is magnetic resonance imaging that we obtained just a week ago reports that his brain has been shattered by cerebral-vascular accidents, by small infarcts, the cortex of his brain is atrophied. We present to you, your Honours, that whatever the Professor Kovacevic from Yugoslavia has said in his statement has been finally confirmed. Many mental state tests that he has submitted are evidenced by the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I have a note. The interpreters are having difficulty keeping up with you. Could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I certainly would. Your Honour, Dr. Kovacevic is indeed a very sick man, but his sickness is not of a nature that cannot be remedied. This is not organic psychosis which is going to go on indefinitely. This is depression to the reaction to all the entireties of the conditions and circumstances that he is in. If he is being given a chance to spend some time, and temporary time, with his family, he would be eternally grateful, grateful in order to come back and have his day in court. This is not -- he wants to get better, to come back, to have his chance to give his side of the story. He does not want to languish in prison and become a vegetable or a victim of his own hand. Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, before I finish, I would like to give the podium over to my co-counsel Pantelic to expand a little bit on the letter by Ms. President Plavsic, because he has some knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I leave the floor, I just have one more exhibit, and the final one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have the Prosecution seen this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I am just handing it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a copy for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit is just a copy of a nurse's notes from detention unit that we have received just yesterday and those are the daily entries of Dr. Kovacevic's blood pressure. The nurse has been so kind and I have for the court brought the original in in the nurse's handwriting and they indicate basically from 3rd October until a few days ago, his blood pressure reading, not a single one has been within the normal limits, notwithstanding all the efforts, so if we go back to the conclusion of Dr. Haeck, Prosecutor's expert witness, that his condition could not be remedied under the conditions of the detention. This is fully supported with a detailed record of Dr. Sommerfeldt from Texas. Your Honour, respectfully I ask you to grant this temporary and short provisional release on humanitarian grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, what was it you wanted to add, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is just a few minutes explanation about some particular conditions and situation that we have in the Prijedor area which might help you having a general approach to this matter for a possible grant of our request. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will hear you, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, generally we are all agreed upon the main aim of Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which is based on general principles for flow and relevant international comments as well as on a common recognised tenderance of human rights. The common conclusion can be made that in all previous cases relevant to Trial Chamber in general terms, the following legal standards are applicable to this particular case of Dr. Kovacevic can be met before. They are the following. The object of Rule 65 is to ensure the presence at the trial of an accused granted provisional release. Next, there is no general rule as to what constitutes an exceptional circumstance. Each application must be determined in the light of its particular circumstances. Provisional release maybe ordered only in very rare cases, such as incompatibility of the health of the accused with any form of detention. The extreme gravity of the current medical condition of the accused is not compatible with any form of detention. The International Tribunal must interpret its rules within its own legal framework. The Trial Chamber does not assume that everyone charged with a crime under the Statute will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- if released, present a danger to victims or witnesses or others. Your Honours, this was only a brief presentation of some legal findings in previous decisions of Trial Chamber of this Tribunal. Allow me to bring your attention to some specific facts with regard to present case. First of all, speaking about exceptional circumstances, both parties more or less are agreed upon the fact that if the health of an accused is the basis for a request for provisional release, all other issues such as reasonable suspicion, length of detention, et cetera, which my distinguished colleague Mr. Vucicevic stressed, is not on first, as I can say, place. My distinguished colleague Mr. Vucicevic has brought to your attention all relevant facts related to the state of health of Dr. Milan Kovacevic. I guess we can not oppose these factual medical findings that sharply shows us the level and the state of the health of Mr. Kovacevic. In order to satisfy Trial Chamber that Mr. Kovacevic is willing to appear for trial, if the request for provisional release will be granted, the Defence has proved by various official documents and statements that there are no obstacles on the side of official institutions of Republika Srpska with regard to the appearance of Mr. Kovacevic before this Trial Chamber. Furthermore, let me bring to your attention some brief explanation regarding one part of the supporting material of the Prosecutor's response dated January 14th. The Prosecutor attached to his response the letter dated January 2nd 1997, signed by the President of Republika Srpska, Madam Biljana Plavsic, which is addressed to the Secretary General of the UN, Mr. Koffi Anan, as well as to Ambassadors of the member states of the Security Council, explaining the actual position of Republika Srpska at that time, particularly January 2nd 1997. I am absolutely convinced that not only the Prosecutor but also all in this courtroom are fully aware that from the very beginning of last year when this letter was made, many significant changes have been made in political life of Republika Srpska and also in position of international community toward political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and notably toward Republika Srpska. We all very well know that Madam Plavsic, the President of Republika Srpska, is fully recognised by the official of international community and also by the representatives of international community in Bosnia-Herzegovina as she is a key factor, key subject and person for fulfilment of all obligation arising from Dayton peace accord. In terms of obligation of the institution of Republika Srpska toward this particular case and possible assistance of local police forces acting in Prijedor area, the Defence can assure this Trial Chamber that all necessary police assistance, in order to fulfil obligations from this Trial Chamber will be provided immediately and with undue delay. In support of this fact, let me remind you that the local police of Prijedor was very co-operative in recent action which was initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor in Prijedor area, Prijedor town, and which was exercised last month. Local police station -- I mean, this action was made in order to obtain some documents in municipality of Prijedor, SDS Party premises, and the local police offices. This fact shows us a high level of commitment of full, relevant political factors of Republika Srpska, notably in this region, with regard to co-operation with the Tribunal and the whole process of implementation of Dayton peace accord. If granted, this request for provisional release of Dr. Milan Kovacevic will not prove only the ability of the Tribunal but will also be a milestone, in my point of view, in support of persons fully committed to obligations arising from Dayton peace accord, which I see in the personality of Madam Plavsic, the President of Republika Srpska and the executives which are lawyer to her, including Minister of Police, Mr. Pavic. This Tribunal should go forward by supporting of peace process in Bosnia, and I see this case as a possible positive effort, if this honourable Trial Chamber granted our request for provisional release of Mr. Kovacevic. Finally, my guess is that by granting this request for provisional release in this case, the Tribunal has an unique opportunity to encourage some of the indicted persons residing in Republika Srpska to surrender themselves to the Tribunal, because this possible positive decision of this Trial Chamber in this case, from my point of view, will have a tremendous influence on them to do and to act in order to surrender themselves here and also generally to justice. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keegan, do you want to add anything? If so, would you have an eye on the clock? We will be taking a break some time shortly after 3.30 and if you could conclude your submissions by then, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. I will certainly try. The submissions by the Prosecution, your Honours, I believe cover the main points that are in issue here today. Those are, of course, that Rules 64 and 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in fact require detention upon the transfer and surrender of a person to the Tribunal and that release from that detention may only be granted if all of the criteria flowing from Rule 65 will met. The decision in the Delalic case, which has been followed by the subsequent cases of Blaskic and Landzo, the decisions there, indicate that even if the criteria are met, the question of release is still a discretionary matter for the Trial Chamber; conversely, that if any one of the criteria is not met, release cannot be granted. It is also clear that the criteria of Rule 65 must be established by facts to the satisfaction of the Trial Chamber; facts, of course, equivalent to evidence, if you will. I would note today that we have had a tremendous amount of assertions by counsel. The only facts or evidence presented are those particular pages that purport to be medical records from Prijedor and now this sheet of paper that apparently is a blood pressure reading record. These submissions of counsel, of course, are not evidence and should not be considered in determining whether the criteria are met. They certainly may be used to explain evidence and considered as such, but they are certainly not facts in and of themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you can take it that we have that point well in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That being the case, it is only now for the Prosecution to respond to the facts raised by the Defence, if in fact the Trial Chamber finds that the Defence through that submission has reasonably raised the issue, or if I put it into converse, reasonably raised a doubt about the existence of a reasonable basis for the detention, as we indicated in our submission, and I believe that as it flows directly from the Delalic decision, the question of whether the Trial Chamber needs to address the issue of this reasonable cause for detention only exists if the Defence causes a doubt about that issue; in other words, if they introduce sufficient evidence that would cause the Trial Chamber to question the original confirmation of the indictment, that is the determination of a reasonable cause, which is the basis for the original detention. We do not believe, in our submission, that this information brought forward by the Defence here today does raise any reasonable doubt as to the original determination of a prima facie case against this accused by a judge of the Tribunal upon confirmation of the indictment. However, in the event that this Trial Chamber does find that the submission of any information requires a response by the Prosecution, we have prepared some additional exhibits, because of the fact that despite the assertions of the Defence counsel, this Trial Chamber, of course, has no information or evidence regarding the case of the accused before it at this time. Therefore we have prepared some exhibits which respond directly to the issues raised by the Defence by their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, before you submit those, there is just a matter I want to raise with my colleagues. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, we need not trouble you. Mr. Keegan, we are not going to see any more evidence. We have enough, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In that instance, sir, I will move on quickly to the various issues. We do not believe, as indicated in our response, that the Defence has met their burden on any of the criteria, the first being the indication of the medical condition of the accused as amounting to an exceptional circumstance. Even if we take the Defence position as stated, as the accurate assessment of the state of the accused's health, nothing about the fact that the accused has a hard condition, nor that he may be depressed because of his current circumstances, amounts to an exceptional circumstance. Both those conditions may be treated either at the detention unit itself or certainly at a hospital somewhere here in the Netherlands if necessary, as in fact has been done already in this case. Nothing about that circumstance requires a release from detention to effect medical treatment. That is consistent with the holding, of course, in the Delic case, which was cited in our brief. If in fact we then move on, away from the medical condition as not amounting to an exceptional circumstance, the Defence has also now raised, of course, this issue of doubt of a reasonable basis and you have the submissions from the parties on that. If in fact that fails -- in point of fact, there is no need to go any further, because you have now failed on one of the criteria and given the jurisprudence of this Tribunal on Rule 65 that in itself would end the discussion. As soon as any one of the criteria has failed to be met by the Defence, we need not discuss any other issues. However, I would just like to briefly touch on the following issues. The question of -- sorry, I will slow down. The question of whether the accused is a flight risk. Again, the Defence has presented no evidence as to that issue. We have submissions by counsel, we have in fact no evidence. On the contrary, we do have indications that by virtue of the indictment in this case, that this accused has been charged with what is considered by most perhaps a most egregious crime against humanity, genocide, or complicit in genocide, to be specific in this case. The nature of the crimes committed in the course of that conduct would indicate, and his involvement in such conduct, would indicate that there is a very direct threat just based on the serious nature of the charges, there is the potential for a threat to witnesses. In fact, if this accused was released and would be gaining continuing knowledge of the case by virtue of the disclosure process would put specific individuals at risk, which may or may not be known to his co-actors. In addition to the submissions by Defence on the current state of co-operation from Republika Srpska, as we noted in our brief, there are still 48 accused, none of which have been turned over or arrested, and you have the letter from Madam Plavsic which indicates they find a legal obstacle to any cases brought at this time, that they are ultra vires of the authority of this Tribunal. You also have the fact that the most recent letter submitted by the Defence says nothing about guarantees for ensuring that this accused would return for trial. It simply says, "we understand he is sick, please send him home to his family". Moving on to the issue, the final issue, then, of the effect on witnesses, we think it is clear also from the prior cases and their analysis of this issue, the provisional release of the accused under these circumstances, where there is nothing to justify such a release, would certainly have a deleterious effect on the administration of justice in this Tribunal and in this case in particular. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Anything you would like to add, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan's speculation as far as Dr. Kovacevic's possible intimidation of the witnesses, it is unfounded. Dr. Kovacevic has never done anything to intimidate anybody before and in the case that we submitted in our brief, US versus Gallow, a co-conspirator in an organised family, crime family, has been released because the court found that if there was an intent to harm the witnesses, the accused could harm witnesses right from the jail where he is, so combined with the fact that there are alleged co-conspirators out at large, allowing Dr. Kovacevic to return temporarily to his home to give a chance to his treatment to take hold and to bring him back where he should be to face this trial is quite humanitarian and statements of the Prosecutor are self-serving and, even more, to a degree, to justify further holding of the defendant against whom the evidence does not support further detention. He is very sick. When the other detainees go out there in a caged courtyard to play ball, he cannot do anything. He always stands and watches. Cannot he flee? This is not supported by the medical evidence. These are conclusions, self-serving conclusions. Mr. Keegan, in commenting on the medical treatment in our submissions, actually in our reiterations of the facts, your Honours, every fact that I brought before you in my statement is contained in the reports. None of those were submissions, but yet, the Prosecutor says his condition of heart and his hypertension could be treated in the local hospitals if not in the jail. If that is the case, why was not that done within the last seven months? The Prosecutor is well within his discretion to help to a proper treatment, but nothing has been done. Perhaps if Dr. Kovacevic dies by the act of God with a chance of 30 to 40 per cent, or take his own life as Socrates did, whose works does he read, the Prosecution would be relieved, because they will not have to prove the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I do not think that is a fair point, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not say that it is the intent of the Prosecution, your Honour. I did not say that as the offence to anybody, but it comes out as a logical conclusion, your Honour, but reason and logic are the essence of law, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. I am going to make an enquiry about the usual length of these adjournments. We will consider this case and we will adjourn for 20 minutes to do so. (3.30 pm) (A short break) (3.50 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rule 65 provides that release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances, and only if it is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial, and if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person. We have considered this motion. We have considered the evidence and the submissions, both oral and in writing, and we have come to the conclusion that we do not find exceptional circumstances in this case, and accordingly, this motion for provisional release is refused. We shall give our reasons in writing at a later date. That ends the hearing as far as this motion is concerned, but as I indicated on an earlier occasion, there are matters about the procedure in this case which need to be discussed. Accordingly, there will be a Status Conference, but it will have to take place, as is normal, in closed session, so we will rise while that is prepared and then we will have the Status Conference. (3.55 pm)
